facts.text: Compute cost is the cost of running simulations, determined by the computer's hourly price, the hours it runs, and the simulated time produced per computer hour.
facts.quote: Compute cost is what it costs to run the simulations, and it is set by three numbers: the price per hour of the computer, how many hours it runs, and how much simulated time each hour produces.

facts.text: Simulation cost per simulated hour equals the cloud price per wall-clock hour divided by the real-time factor (RTF), where RTF is simulated seconds produced per wall-clock second.
facts.quote: cost per simulated hour equals the cloud price per wall-clock hour divided by the real-time factor.

facts.text: At the same hourly computer price, a simulator running at 10 times real time costs one tenth as much per simulated hour as a real-time simulator; a simulator running at 0.1 times real time costs ten times as much.
facts.quote: A tool at 10 times real time therefore costs one tenth as much per simulated hour as one at real time, and one at 0.1 times costs ten times as much

facts.text: To estimate the number of simulation runs affordable within a budget, divide the budget by hourly computer price, multiply the resulting purchased hours by RTF, and divide the resulting simulated hours by one scenario's duration.
facts.quote: hours bought equals budget divided by hourly price; simulated hours equals hours bought times RTF; runs equals simulated hours divided by the length of one scenario.

facts.text: The booklet's compute-budget example uses ten cloud instances with one GPU each, running 24 hours a day for 122 days, to obtain about 29,000 GPU-hours for about USD 54,490 on demand.
facts.quote: ten cloud instances, each with one graphics processing unit (GPU), running 24 hours a day for 122 days give about 29,000 GPU-hours for about USD 54,490 on demand.

facts.text: If sensor-realistic simulation runs near real time, the booklet's 29,000-GPU-hour example yields roughly 29,000 hours of simulated driving; this limits full-fidelity coverage of 100-plus sites multiplied by 10-plus scenarios, weather conditions and machine variants, forcing a tiered strategy.
facts.quote: roughly 29,000 hours of simulated driving, which caps how many of the 100-plus sites times 10-plus scenarios times weather times machine variants can run at full fidelity and forces a tiered strategy

facts.text: The booklet's reference compute-cost table estimates 1,000 GPU-hours at about USD 1,734–1,861, excluding licenses, storage, network traffic and support.
The booklet's reference compute-cost table estimates 10,000 GPU-hours at about USD 17,344–18,610, excluding licenses, storage, network traffic and support.
The booklet's reference compute-cost table estimates 100,000 GPU-hours at about USD 173,438–186,100, excluding licenses, storage, network traffic and support.
facts.quote: 100,000 about USD 173,438 to 186,100, excluding licenses, storage, network traffic and support.

facts.text: A radar solver running on a CPU took 14 hours to simulate a 12-second scenario, corresponding to an RTF of about 0.0002.
facts.quote: A radar solver on a central processor (CPU) took 14 hours to simulate a 12-second scenario, an RTF of about 0.0002

facts.text: The GPU version of the vendor method used for the CPU radar-solver example produced a frame in about 12 milliseconds.
facts.quote: the GPU version of the same vendor's method produced a frame in about 12 milliseconds.

facts.text: Chrono's continuum soil simulation runs 50–200 times slower than real time.
facts.quote: Chrono's continuum soil runs 50 to 200 times slower than real time

facts.text: The booklet concludes that compute is cheap relative to engineering labor, estimated at roughly USD 150,000–260,000 per specialist per year.
facts.quote: Compute is cheap relative to engineering labor, which the booklet puts at roughly USD 150,000 to 260,000 per specialist per year.

facts.text: The booklet identifies model preparation, correlation measurements and human triage of failures as larger risks than compute cost, and recommends benchmarking these activities end to end before scaling infrastructure.
facts.quote: The larger risks it names are model preparation, correlation measurements and human triage of failures, to be benchmarked end to end before scaling infrastructure
